How does gender affect the effectiveness of public sector interventions? Evidence for Colombia
https://www.nber.org/papers/w22998
We investigate whether gender differences in vulnerability to and impacts of droughts explain variation in the effectiveness of safety net programs. We study the impacts of a national program designed to combat poverty and malnutrition in Colombia from 2009–2011 using both survey responses and geospatial variation in vulnerability. We find that program participation alleviates food insecurity during droughts, and that the impacts are larger for women than for men. These findings suggest that men and women have different reactions to droughts, and that interventions targeting the more vulnerable segments of the population can be more effective when targeting women.
Treatment programs can vary in efficacy largely due to variation in the target population and the implementation context. In many cases, gender is one important aspect to consider when estimating welfare impacts. We explore the implications of this by studying the effectiveness of a social protection program in Colombia from 2009 to 2011. The government implemented a series of actions in conjunction with the 2008 drought to combat poverty and malnutrition through a program called Programa de Promoción Social para la Productividad e inclusión (PRONAPRODEN). Our contribution is twofold: First, we show that PRONAPRODEN significantly reduced food insecurity, with the impacts being larger for women than for men in drought-affected municipalities. Second, we document differential impacts by gender and drought severity over the six years of program implementation, suggesting that gender differences in drought-related vulnerabilities may explain why the program worked better during some years than others. These findings provide evidence that gender could be considered when evaluating the effectiveness of program interventions. They also suggest that efforts to improve the reach and coverage of social programs can be more successful if targeting women.
The program we study is an unconditional social protection program, meaning it did not target low-income individuals (those who fall below a certain threshold on a pre-defined measure of poverty).1 Instead, all individuals living in PRONAPRODEN municipalities, regardless of their asset or income levels, were granted annual transfers of up to $50 per adult per month for five years.2 PRONAPRODEN was designed to reach households that are vulnerable to food insecurity, specifically through the implementation of a "targeting tool" that allowed for conditional targeting.3
